Quick answer: Dussehra (Vijayadashami) celebrates two victories at once: Lord Rama 's victory over Ravana, told in the Ramayana , and Goddess Durga 's victory over the buffalo-demon Mahishasura, told in the Devi Mahatmya. North and west India mostly remember Rama with Ramlila and Ravana Dahan; eastern India mostly remembers Durga at the end of Durga Puja. Both stories carry one message: dharma wins in the end. In 2026, Vijayadashami was on Tuesday 20 October (Drik Panchang )

Rama, prince of Ayodhya, went into fourteen years of forest exile to keep his father Dasharatha's promise, with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana. While they lived at Panchavati, Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka, sent the demon Maricha in the form of a golden deer to lure the brothers away. Ravana then carried Sita off in his aerial chariot. The old vulture Jatayu fought to stop him and was mortally wounded
Advertisement
Hanuman, Sugriva and the bridge to Lanka
Searching for Sita, Rama and Lakshmana met Hanuman and the vanara king Sugriva in Kishkindha. Hanuman leapt across the sea, found Sita in Ravana's Ashoka grove, gave her Rama's ring and, before returning, set Lanka on fire with his burning tail. Ravana's brother Vibhishana advised him to return Sita; when Ravana refused, Vibhishana crossed over to Rama. The vanara army then built a bridge (setu) to Lanka under the direction of Nala
Advertisement
The war and the fall of Ravana
In the long war, Ravana's brother Kumbhakarna and his son Indrajit fell, Indrajit at Lakshmana's hands. When Rama stood weary before the final battle with Ravana, the sage Agastya came to him and taught him the Aditya Hridayam, a hymn to the Sun. Its opening verses describe that moment

Frequently asked questions
What is the story behind Dussehra?
As commonly told, Dussehra celebrates two victories: Lord Rama defeating Ravana, the king of Lanka, as told in the Ramayana, and Goddess Durga slaying the buffalo-demon Mahishasura, as told in the Devi Mahatmya. Both mark the triumph of dharma on the tenth day
Why did Lord Rama fight Ravana?
Ravana carried Sita away from the forest hermitage at Panchavati. Rama, with Lakshmana, Hanuman, Sugriva's army and Vibhishana, crossed to Lanka and fought to bring her back after Ravana refused to return her
How did Goddess Durga defeat Mahishasura?
In the Devi Mahatmya, the radiance of all the gods joins to form the Devi, and each god gives her a weapon. Mahishasura changes form again and again, as buffalo, lion, man and elephant, until the Devi pins him down, pierces him with her trident and cuts off his head
Which scriptures tell the two Dussehra stories?
Rama's war with Ravana is told in the Yuddha Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana and in later versions such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Durga's victory over Mahishasura is told in chapters 2 to 4 of the Devi Mahatmya, part of the Markandeya Purana

The Ramayana predates written history. Valmiki’s Sanskrit version is the earliest text, but oral traditions reach back further. The epic was retold across Asia: the Thai Ramakien , the Indonesian Kakawin Ramayana , the Cambodian Reamker . In each, the core remains: a king who overreaches, a prince who restores order
By the 16th century, Tulsidas composed the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a vernacular Hindi. This version became the devotional standard for northern India. In it, Rama is not just a prince but God himself, and Ravana’s sin is not simply kidnapping Sita but the arrogance of placing himself above the divine
The battle is fought on a precise geography. Lanka is described as a golden city on a mountain, surrounded by a moat of fire. The bridge Rama builds — the Rama Setu — is still debated by geologists. Some say it is a natural formation. Others say it was built
Rama and Ravana as Two Selves
Esoteric Hinduism reads the Ramayana as a map of the psyche. Rama is the jivatman (the individual soul) governed by dharma. Ravana is the ahamkara (the ego) with its ten heads: the five jnanendriyas (senses of perception) and five karmendriyas (organs of action). The ten heads are not a deformity. They are a catalogue of hunger

A Brahmin scholar with ten heads, master of the Vedas, inventor of the veena , and the only being Shiva ever called “my son,” once dragged a woman by her hair across a courtyard. That woman was Sita. That scholar was Ravana. And the war that followed was not a war between good and evil. It was a war between two men who both knew the scriptures, who both had performed austerities, and who both believed they were right
Rama wins the battle against Ravana, but the victory is not a simple triumph of light over darkness. It is the exhaustion of a karmic debt, the end of a cycle that began long before the war, and the final lesson in a spiritual anatomy that Indian esoteric traditions have mapped for centuries
Meta: The Ramayana war between Rama and Ravana is the central epic conflict of Hindu mythology, but esoteric traditions read it as an allegory of the inner battle between the disciplined soul and the ten-headed mind

Primary antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana
Several terms redirect here. For other uses, see Ravan (disambiguation)
Ravana ( Sanskrit : रावण , romanized : Rāvaṇa , lit. ' roaring ' ) is the principal antagonist of the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana and its several other versions . He is traditionally depicted as a ten-headed rakshasa (demon) king of Lanka . In the Ramayana , Ravana is described as the eldest son of sage Vishrava and Kaikasi . He abducted Rama 's wife, Sita , and took her to his kingdom of Lanka, where he held her in the Ashoka Vatika . Rama, with the support of vanara King Sugriva and his army of vanaras, launched a rescue operation for Sita against Ravana in Lanka. Ravana was subsequently slain, and Rama rescued his beloved wife Sita. His epic defeat is celebrated yearly by burning a large effigy, depicting the ten-headed Ravana, during the Hindu festival of Dussehra
Ravana was well-versed in the six shastras and the four Vedas , including the Shiva Tandava Stotra . Ravana is also considered to be an ardent devotee of Shiva . Images of Ravana are often seen associated with Shiva at temples. He also appears in the Buddhist Mahayana text Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra , in Buddhist Jatakas , as well as in Jain Ramayanas . In Vaishnava scriptures , he is depicted as one of Vishnu 's cursed doorkeepers

The narrator says again that every person who Ravana sent into battle didn't return. Ravana stands in a tower and watches the battle for a while. The carnage makes him exceptionally angry. He performs ritual prayers, dresses in his armor, and when he's dressed, he looks very heroic. Ravana summons his chariot and vows that at the end of the day, either Sita or Ravana's own wife will be a widow
The narration creates a sense of dread by making it extremely clear that Ravana is fighting a losing battle. Though Ravana is described as looking heroic, the story has already shown that looking heroic isn't at all the same as acting heroic. This connects to Ravana's love of show and display, however

Ravana 's resolve attracts the attention of the gods, and they send down Indra 's chariot to help Rama . The charioteer introduces himself as Matali , and explains that the gods Indra, Brahma , and Shiva sent him to help Rama, and he lists the chariot's special powers. Rama wonders aloud if the rakshasas sent Matali as a trap, but both Hanuman and Lakshmana insist that the chariot is real. Rama gathers his weapons and climbs into the chariot

He is credited as the author of the Arka Prakasha, a foundational Sanskrit compendium on the science of distillation . In this text, Ravana describes the extraction of volatile oils and aromatic essences which is a method used to preserve the Virya (potency) of plants that might otherwise be degraded by standard decoction (Kwatha) methods. Additionally, traditional accounts attribute works on Ayurvedic Alchemy ( Rasashastra ) and pulse diagnosis (Nadi Pariksha) to him, establishing his significance within the Vedic medical lineage. In some later versions, he is said to have possessed the nectar of immortality, which was stored inside his belly thanks to a celestial boon from Brahma . In the War with Lord Rama, Ravana was killed by a powerful Brahma's weapon shot by Rama which was gifted to Rama by Sage Agstya

But the practice is older than the pyrotechnics. Villages across India perform Ramlila , a dramatic reenactment of the Ramayana that can last nine days or a month. The actors are often local men who have taken vows of purity during the performance. The actor playing Ravana must fast, avoid certain foods, and meditate on the king’s arrogance as a warning
Temples dedicated to Ravana are rare but exist. In Bisrakh, Uttar Pradesh, a temple honors Ravana as a local ancestor. In Mandu, Madhya Pradesh, a shrine marks the site where his wife, Mandodari, is said to have meditated. These are not contradictions. They are reminders that the Ramayana is a story about a man, not a monster
In esoteric traditions, the recitation of the Ramayana itself is a sadhana (spiritual practice). The Rama Taraka Mantra (“Ram”) is chanted to purify the mind. The name of Rama is said to burn through karma like the arrow through Ravana’s navel

ranked_evidence.text:
Epics The Western reader might compare the Ramayana to the Iliad . Both involve a war over a woman. Both end with a city destroyed. But the difference is crucial
In the Iliad , Achilles fights for glory and grief. In the Ramayana, Rama fights because he must. He has no rage. He offers Ravana multiple chances to surrender. Even after Ravana dies, Rama weeps for him and tells his brother Lakshmana to learn from Ravana’s wisdom. The enemy is not a villain. He is a teacher whose lesson is paid in death
The closest parallel in Western esotericism is the Mabinogion or the Chanson de Roland , but neither contains the same moral ambiguity. The Bhagavad Gita , another Hindu text, is a more direct parallel: Arjuna, like Rama, faces enemies who are his own family. But the Gita stops at the edge of the battlefield. The Ramayana crosses it
In Zoroastrianism, the battle between Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu is a cosmic war of light and darkness. The Ramayana refuses this dualism. Ravana is a devotee of Shiva. He does not hate the gods. He simply wants everything. The war is not between two worlds but between two versions of the same world

Brahmins of Gujarat claim to be descendants of Ravana, and sometimes have "Ravan" as their surnames Saraswat Brahmins from Mathura claim Ravana as a saraswat Brahmin as per his lineage
The Gondi people of central India claim to be descendants of Ravana, and have temples for him, his wife Mandodari, and their son Meghnad. They also state that Ravana was an ancient Gond king, the tenth dharmaguru of their tribe, and the eighteenth lingo (divine teacher). Annually on Dussehra , the Gondis from the village of Paraswadi carry an image of Ravana riding on an elephant in a procession. He is also worshipped by the Nihali people
Temples

Influence on culture and art
Ravana with Hanuman in tholu bommalata , a shadow puppet tradition of Andhra Pradesh , India
Ravana-Dahan (burning effigy of Ravana)
An effigy of Ravana with burning sparklers on Dusshera . Dashehra Diwali Mela in Manchester, England, 2006
Effigies of Ravana are burned on Vijayadashami in many places throughout India to symbolize Rama's triumph over evil
Ravanahatha
According to mythology, the ravanahatha , an ancient bowed string instrument , was created by Ravana and is still used as a Rajasthani folk instrument

Ravana and his two brothers, Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana , performed penance on Mount Gokarna for 10,000 years and won boons from Brahma. Ravana was blessed with a boon that would make him invincible to all the creations of Brahma, except for humans. He also received weapons, a chariot, as well as the ability to shapeshift from Brahma. According to the Ramayana , demigods approached Brahma since Ravana was causing harm on Earth. Lord Vishnu appeared and gave blessings that Rama would incarnate as a human and kill Ravana since his invincibility boon did not include humans

Immolation of Vedavati
Ravana found Vedavati sitting in meditation as a tapasvini and was captivated by her beauty. He proposed his hand in marriage to her, and was rejected. Ravana, firmly rejected at every turn, grabbed her hair and tried assaulting her. The furious Vedavati cursed Ravana that she would be born once more, and would be the cause of his death. She subsequently leapt into the ritual havan that was present in her vicinity, immolating herself
